caption:
If I was starting to build my financial literacy in my late 20s, here’s the 20 most important things I’d start with ⭐️

1. Open up an investing account (in 🇨🇦: TFSA // in 🇺🇸: Roth IRA), put in $20 to start and buy a fractional share of an all-in-one ETF

(Comment INVEST if you’d like the investing platform I use, which also gets you $25 to start)

2. Learn the 50/30/20 basic budgeting rule and slowly adjust to your own goals afterwards.

3. Use a budgeting app or spreadsheet to start tracking your money and where it all should be going. (If you need a spreadsheet, let me know and I will send you mine)

4. Lock in and build a 6-month emergency fund in a high interest savings account. To calculate this get [$x monthly expenses] x 6.

5. Understand how compound interest works!! It’s the 8th wonder of the world for a REASON (use an online calculator to see how the numbers grow)

6. Learn about the registered accounts! In Canada, the TFSA/FHSA/RRSP are the ones you want to know in your 20-30s

7. Look into the 5 factors that make up a credit score and start monitoring your credit score through Borrowell or Credit Karma to get a free report & score

8. Create CLEAR financial goals~ this is the year where you’ll tell yourself “I want to save my first $10K” or “I want to start a payday routine”

9. Pay off debt through the SNOWBALL method or AVALANCHE method (look into what these are & how they might apply to you) 

10. If your taxes aren’t complicated, FILE YOUR OWN TAXES! It saves you $100 from the accountant and it truly isn’t very hard. This is the best way to learn basic tax knowledge because you’re endeavoring a skill

11. Understand that consistency in saving/investing is how you build wealth!! Lump sum investing is proven to deliver better returns but we don’t all have a chunk of money sitting around all the time SO dollar cost averaging is just as good and a routine to get into by setting aside your income regularly 

12. Automate ANYTHING and EVERYTHING — the cheat code to a lazy routine is setting up systems so that you don’t have to think about doing it

stop asking yourself why you’re keeping money you’re not spending. that thought is the enemy. the second you stop acknowledging that account exists, the urge to touch it fades.

2️⃣ it’s not your money…. it’s your future’s
mentally give it to your future self. that person needs it way more than present-you needs a treat. you didn’t even earn it yet!! it’s borrowed confidence.

3️⃣ now make it work harder than you do
move it into a TFSA or high-interest savings (COMMENT TRANSFER for my fave app) and let compound interest do what you can’t! grow it while you sleep. then watch how fast that obsession kicks in.

caption:
FHSA MUST KNOW—Carryforward Rule

This rule has not been emphasized as much as it should be so here I am, hopefully with a simple enough explanation since this is a very confusing concept. Always do your own research and take what you learn online as a search topic!

Here’s why this rule is important:
⚠️ Say that you open the FHSA in 2023 with the hopes of purchasing your first home in 2027 with a limit of $40K ($8K earned each year). You don’t contribute in 2023 and 2024 but plan to contribute a lump sum in the later years. Here’s what would happen👇🏻

In 2023, you have a contribution room of $8000. This gets carried forward to 2024 as there was no contribution.

In 2024, you get a new limit of $8000 and the carryforward room from 2023, totalling a contribution room of $16,000 but no contributions are made.

In 2025, you get a new limit of $8000 and only $8000 is carried forward from 2024, totalling a contribution room of $16,000 (not $24,000). You decide to contribute $8000 in 2025, leaving you with $8000 that you can carryforward to 2026.

In 2026, you have the new limit of $8000 and the carryforward room from 2025 of $8000, totalling $16,000 in contribution room and $8000 already used up. Your total limit is $24,000. You decide to contribute $10,000 in 2026.

In 2027, you get a new limit of $8000 and the carryforward amount of $6000 from 2026, totalling a contribution room of $14,000 left and $18,000 already contributed. Your total limit is $32,000–missing out on $8000 of additional room you could have had towards your first home. 

Did you know this rule?

caption:
I’m a big @vanguardgroup girly 👀 

There’s nothing more to investing than just consistently buying into the stock market that tracks indices like the S&P 500. You don’t need to have a bunch of individual stocks and become an investing nerd to start investing. Just stay consistent and patient with a handful of *good* ETFs and let it compound long-term. 

My fave ETFs are all from Vanguard but there are obviously other ones out there! I learned it the hard way by buying into individual stocks with no research, day trading, options trading and alt coins only to lose a good amount of money. I learned that you don’t really need any of that to be a great investor. If that’s your thing though, all to ya!!

Gen Zs have a time horizon of like 30-40 years. That’s a very long time to grow your wealth for retirement. I want to let the market do it’s thing and let that average annual return of about 10% compound than deciding on individual stocks now. I think this is a big self-realization moment that my risk tolerance is CHANGING✨ That does not mean I’m selling all my individual stocks and rebalancing it to just have ETFs! I will still keep the ones that I did the research for but minimize my holdings. Btw if you want to know which stocks I have, check out my portfolio on @meetblossomsocial 🌸
